title: The EU AI Act: 6 Steps to Take Before 2 August 2026
author: Julia Apostle · Sarah Schaedler

dom.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The source accepts the EU framework’s differentiated, enforceable approach and materially develops the cluster’s practical implementation case through a repeatable programme based on system mapping, risk classification, organisational roles, contracts and continuing cross-functional governance. It offers compliance guidance rather than evidence of regulatory effectiveness.
qs: Understanding the risk classification of AI systems and AI models, as well as the company’s role in relation to these, is the foundation for AI governance (see Step 6).

[For more information regarding open-source GPAIMs, see our article here.]  - Make sure your process for identifying regulated AI systems and GPAIMs is documented and replicable, since this will be an ongoing obligation.

kp.k: Major compliance obligations take effect on 2 August 2026
kp.d: In this November 2025 practitioner guidance, Julia Apostle and Sarah Schaedler state that provisions concerning prohibited AI systems and general-purpose AI models already apply, with most remaining obligations and their enforcement beginning on 2 August 2026. The document recommends corporate compliance preparations rather than reporting empirical findings about legal employment or market restructuring.
qs: The EU AI Act’s provisions have started to apply, including those relating to prohibited AI systems and general-purpose AI models (GPAIM).
The bulk of the remaining obligations take effect on 2 August 2026, and authorities will be able to enforce compliance from that date.

kp.k: AI inventories should capture less visible professional uses
kp.d: The authors recommend department-by-department mapping of systems and models used, developed, imported or distributed, including freely accessible tools. They warn that professional use can trigger transparency obligations and recommend a documented, repeatable identification process because the obligation is ongoing.
qs: Consider a department-by-department approach to help identify less visible use cases.
A growing number of free AI systems are accessible online via APIs and mobile apps. Keep in mind that using those systems for professional purposes can trigger transparency obligations under the Act.
Make sure your process for identifying regulated AI systems and GPAIMs is documented and replicable, since this will be an ongoing obligation.

kp.k: Functionality and model definitions determine regulatory coverage
kp.d: The guidance distinguishes inference-capable AI systems from human-defined rules-based systems, and general-purpose models from systems built on them. It reports Commission guidance treating training compute exceeding 10²³ FLOPs, together with specified generative capabilities, as indicative of a general-purpose model. Companies developing their own models should assess coverage rather than rely on product labels.
qs: Focus on the functionality of any products identified as “AI.”
AI systems are differentiated from other human-defined, rules-based systems that automatically execute operations, which are beyond the scope of the regulation.
The Act imposes obligations on GPAIM developers, so companies that develop their own AI models should determine whether they are covered.

Guidelines published by the European Commission make clear that the Commission will consider two factors as “indicative” that a model is GPAI: whether the model was trained using a level of compute that exceeds a threshold of 10²³ floating point operations (FLOPs) and whether it can also create language, text-to-image or text-to-video=.

kp.k: Obligations differ across AI value-chain roles
kp.d: The authors state that high-risk system providers bear the most obligations, followed by deployers, while importers and distributors have more limited responsibilities and GPAIM obligations attach only to providers. Co-development and additional development of existing products complicate role allocation and may require contractual amendments.
qs: Organizations that provide (i.e., develop) high-risk AI systems have the most legal obligations, followed by deployers. Importers and distributors have more limited responsibilities. Only providers face obligations related to GPAIMs.

Determining the role(s) your organization plays – and the resulting responsibilities – can be tricky, such as when AI products are co-developed or when a company makes additional developments to an existing AI product.

kp.k: EU coverage can extend to non-EU operators
kp.d: The guidance identifies placing systems on the EU market or putting them into service, and placing GPAIMs on the market, as coverage triggers. It states that non-EU providers can be covered and that providers and deployers outside the EU are also covered when system outputs are used in the EU, describing this as an anti-circumvention measure.
qs: AI systems that are “placed on the market” or “put into service” in the EU by a provider.
GPAIMs a provider has “placed on the market.”

The Act can apply to providers based outside the EU if they meet the criteria above. It will also apply to providers and deployers of AI systems based outside the EU if the outputs produced are used in the EU, to avoid circumvention of the Act’s requirements.

kp.k: Exclusions and grandfathering qualify compliance coverage
kp.d: The article describes exclusions for exclusively military, defense or national-security systems, solely scientific research and development systems, and free and open-source systems unless prohibited or high-risk. Separately, it describes partial exemptions for non-systemic-risk GPAIMs meeting Article 53(2) open-source criteria. It also states that grandfathering extends compliance periods for systems marketed in Europe before 2 August 2026 and GPAIMs marketed before 2 August 2025.
qs: Placed on the market, put into service or used exclusively for military or defense or national security purposes.
Developed or put into service solely for scientific research and development.
Released under free and open-source licenses, unless the system is prohibited or high-risk.

GPAIMs that do not have systemic risk and that are made available under open-source licenses that satisfy the criteria set out at Article 53(2) of the AI Act (e.g. parameters and model architecture must be publicly available) will be exempt from certain obligations under the Act.
The Act has a grandfathering provision that extends the period of compliance for AI systems placed on the market in Europe before 2 August 2026, and GPAIMs placed on the market before 2 August 2025.

kp.k: Risk classification determines additional compliance requirements
kp.d: The authors recommend identifying prohibited and high-risk systems while noting that lower-risk systems can still carry obligations. They state that systemic-risk GPAIMs face additional risk identification, mitigation and incident-reporting requirements, and describe the voluntary Code of Practice, which the article dates to August 2025, as particularly detailed on systemic-risk processes.
qs: A company should determine whether any of the AI systems it uses or develops may be classified as prohibited or high risk under the Act. Even lower risk AI systems may still be subject to certain obligations.
GPAIMs with “systemic risk” are subject to additional risk identification and mitigation requirements, along with incident reporting.
Providers of GPAIMs may sign up to the voluntary Code of Practice published in August 2025.
The Code is particularly detailed in relation to the obligations of providers of GPAIM with systemic risk to implement processes for risk identification and mitigation.

kp.k: Contracts must address modifications and shifting compliance responsibility
kp.d: The guidance recommends incorporating AI Act requirements into pending agreements, acquisitions, due diligence and procurement, and reviewing executed agreements affected by ongoing AI developments. A central contractual issue is how far licensed systems or models may be modified or fine-tuned before compliance responsibility shifts from provider to deployer; the authors anticipate changes rather than document completed market-wide practice.
qs: Make sure any in-progress agreements and acquisitions covering AI products will reflect the requirements of the AI Act when the Act comes into force.
This will likely require changes to contract terms as well as due diligence and revised procurement processes.

A key issue to address for both providers and deployers is the extent to which licensed AI systems and GPAIMs can be modified and/or fine-tuned (in the case of GPAIMs) before responsibility for compliance shifts from the provider to the deployer.
You may also have executed agreements that need to be amended to reflect new and ongoing product developments that involve AI technologies.

kp.k: Governance requires leadership, cross-functional participation and AI literacy
kp.d: The authors recommend internal policies and processes aligning AI use and development with organizational priorities and legal duties, supported by senior leadership and contributors across the company. They identify adequate AI literacy for employees and contractors operating systems as both a governance requirement and an obligation effective in February 2025. Governance should also coordinate AI compliance with data protection, product safety and cybersecurity duties.
qs: An effective AI governance framework also requires support from senior leadership.
People with diverse profiles from different parts of the company should contribute to the framework – for example, in the form of an internal AI working group or by conducting relevant risk analyses.

A key element of AI governance includes ensuring an adequate level of AI literacy amongst the employees and contractors that operate AI systems on behalf of your organization; this is also an obligation under the EU AI Act that took effect in February 2025.

Finally, an AI governance framework will also help align AI-related compliance initiatives with overlapping compliance duties, such as those related to data protection, product safety and cybersecurity.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Julia Apostle and Sarah Schaedler claim that the EU AI Act creates differentiated corporate compliance duties requiring ongoing AI identification, risk classification, contractual changes and internal governance.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain corporate AI compliance article, not a prediction about lawyer displacement, law-firm economics or legal-service markets. The authors state that AI obligations depend on an organization's value-chain role, the technology's risk classification and its connection to the EU. They identify professional use of freely accessible AI as a potential trigger for transparency duties and say AI identification must be documented and repeatable. They predict likely changes to contracts, acquisition due diligence and procurement, including addressing when modifications or model fine-tuning shift compliance responsibility from provider to deployer. They also claim that governance helps coordinate AI obligations with data protection, product safety and cybersecurity duties.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on the authors' interpretation of legal and regulatory authorities, not empirical findings about AI adoption or compliance outcomes.
pts.d: Apostle and Schaedler cite and quote the EU AI Act's definitions and discuss its scope, operator categories, risk-based obligations, exemptions and implementation dates. They also invoke European Commission guidelines on AI-system definitions and general-purpose AI models, Article 53(2)'s open-source criteria, and a voluntary Code of Practice described as published in August 2025. Related articles are referenced for further explanation. The predicted contractual and organisational changes are practical legal inferences from these requirements; the article supplies no datasets, benchmarks, case studies or measured results demonstrating those changes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The November 10, 2025 article centres on preparation for August 2, 2026, while distinguishing obligations already in effect and conditional extensions or exemptions.
pts.d: The authors say prohibited-system and GPAIM provisions have started applying, AI literacy duties took effect in February 2025, and most remaining obligations become enforceable on August 2, 2026. They identify grandfathering for AI systems placed on the European market before August 2, 2026 and GPAIMs placed on the market before August 2, 2025, without specifying the extended deadlines. Applicability depends on placing systems or models on the EU market, putting systems into service there, or using certain non-EU operators' system outputs in the EU. They describe exclusions for exclusively military, defence or national-security uses and solely scientific research and development, as well as open-source qualifications. They distinguish system-level open-source exclusions from partial exemptions for qualifying non-systemic-risk open-source GPAIMs. Lower-risk AI can still attract obligations, while systemic-risk GPAIMs attract additional requirements.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected parties are corporate AI operators and their personnel, with obligations varying by role and risk rather than by legal-market segment.
pts.d: The authors identify providers, deployers, importers, distributors and product manufacturers, including qualifying organisations outside the EU. They say high-risk-system providers bear the most obligations, followed by deployers, while importers and distributors have more limited responsibilities; GPAIM-specific obligations attach only to providers. Systemic-risk GPAIM providers face additional risk identification, mitigation and incident reporting. Co-developers and companies modifying existing AI products may need to clarify responsibilities and amend agreements. Procurement and acquisition processes must account for AI requirements. Senior leadership and cross-functional personnel are expected to support governance, and employees and contractors operating AI require adequate literacy. The article does not separately identify law firms, ALSPs or legal clients as affected segments.
